# Goethe — Permanence in Change

## #0

<a id="goethe-blossom-and-shade"></a>

The speaker asks for one hour in which the early blessing could be held. Already the mild west wind shakes down a shower of blossom. The force carrying beauty away is gentle. The loss begins within the weather that belongs to its flourishing.

Green foliage offers another occasion for pleasure. Its shade has just been enjoyed, but the speaker sees autumn within that present gift: the leaves will turn pale and a storm will scatter them. The opening eight lines of *Dauer im Wechsel* move through a wish, an accomplished loss, a question about enjoyment and an anticipated loss. Spring's passing is felt from inside the pleasure it gives. The speaker's question concerns how to receive something whose passing has already entered the reception.

This whole follows all forty German lines in the [Klett 2010 witness](https://www2.klett.de/sixcms/media.php/229/350470_0239_Goethe_Dauer.pdf), which identifies its source as the Frankfurt edition of Goethe's works, I.2, *Gedichte 1800–1832* (1988), pp. 78–79. The [canonical source house](../../../../episteme/sources/literature/goethe/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims.md) distinguishes that German witness from John Frederick Nims's selected 1983 translation, whose page 169 remains uncollated. “Permanence and Change” is this project's admitted alias of the same poem. The present account uses the German whole; it does not supply or impersonate Nims's translation.

## #1

<a id="goethe-fruit-valley-river"></a>

The second stanza answers the wish to hold with an instruction to take one's share. Whoever wants the fruit must reach for it promptly. Ripening and germination overlap: while one growth approaches fulfilment, another has begun. What passes therefore includes both the loss of a present gift and the advent of another. The imperative concerns participation in that particular ripening. Waiting for a moment secured against change would miss what is available to be taken.

Rain enlarges the movement from plant to landscape. Every downpour changes the beloved valley. The place remains recognisable enough to be addressed as one's own, yet affection gives no exemption from its alteration. Then the stanza enters the river: one does not swim in the same river a second time. The swimmer participates bodily in what has been observed from the shade and the bank. Water carries the scene forward through a medium that cannot be kept for a repeat encounter.

These eight lines retain several temporal movements together. Fruit has its moment of readiness; germination begins beside it; rain changes the valley through repeated events; swimming cannot recover the same encounter. These different ways of arriving, receiving and passing prepare the poem's next turn, when the one who notices change becomes its subject. [German whole, lines 9–16; source and witness](../../../../episteme/sources/literature/goethe/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims.md#passages).

## #2

<a id="goethe-changing-eyes-and-limbs"></a>

The poem turns directly upon the addressee. Walls and palaces appear rock-solid, but they are continually seen with different eyes. Recognition has a history on the observer's side. The apparently enduring object cannot secure an identical experience of it when the person looking has changed.

The stanza then leaves the spectator's eyes for bodily powers remembered through their acts. The lip that once found healing in a kiss has passed away. So has the foot that tested itself against the cliff with the boldness of a chamois. Intimacy and daring make the body's alteration particular. These are losses of ways of meeting the world: receiving a kiss, trusting one's footing, answering a height with movement.

The cliff and the built walls perform different offices. The walls occasion the recognition that seeing changes; the cliff recalls a bodily capacity that could once meet its challenge. Neither image provides an immovable observer outside the changes being described. The poem has carried the person who wanted to retain the blossom into the very loss that desire first placed before itself. [German whole, lines 17–24](../../../../episteme/sources/literature/goethe/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims.md#passages).

## #3

<a id="goethe-hand-name-and-wave"></a>

The fourth stanza continues the body across the stanza break. The hand once moved willingly and gently to do good. Its remembered value lies in that action. The poem gathers lip, foot and hand into the articulated bodily form and declares it all changed. Kindness belongs to the history of this body alongside pleasure and daring; physical change reaches the means by which those acts became possible.

Then the name remains at the place where its bearer has altered. What now calls itself by that name has arrived like a wave and hurries toward the element. Water now enters the description of the named person. A recognisable designation continues across a succession that it cannot arrest.

The wave is momentarily distinct enough to be encountered and named, while its arrival and departure belong to the element. The poem does not narrate the old body returning unchanged. Nor does a continued name restore the vanished lip, foot or hand. By the end of line 32, the question of duration includes the bodily bearer of the question. The last stanza must answer from within that condition. [German whole, lines 25–32](../../../../episteme/sources/literature/goethe/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims.md#passages).

## #4

<a id="goethe-beginning-end-muses"></a>

The final stanza gives another imperative. Beginning and end are to draw together into one, faster than the objects themselves flee past the addressee. The opening asked that an early blessing stay for an hour. The ending asks for an act of gathering across its passage. What has been separated in time can be brought into a relation that holds beginning and end together.

The Muses enter at this point. Their favour promises something imperishable, and the addressee is asked to give thanks. The closing lines distinguish what is carried in the breast from its form in the mind:

> Den Gehalt in deinem Busen  
> Und die Form in deinem Geist.

The content borne inwardly and the form through which it is apprehended have distinct places in the closing address. The Muses give this gathering an artistic office. The poem itself has brought blossom, fruit, valley, swimmer, changing eyes, bodily acts and the named wave into one formed sequence. Its ending can receive the beginning because the intervening losses have been articulated.

The promise remains a promise of the Muses. The lyric supplies no sequel in which the aging person recovers the earlier body or the valley stops changing. Its continuation is given through what the closing distinction makes available: an inwardly borne content and a formed expression that can carry the relation onward. The opening wish for duration returns changed by the poem that has answered it. [German whole, lines 33–40; verified German closing words](../../../../episteme/sources/literature/goethe/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims/goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims.md#goethe-1983-selected-poems-nims-q002).

## #5→0

The shared [Neumann whole](../../../archetypal-ground/neumann-images/WHOLE.md#neumann-paper-eightfold) **grounds** the A11/A12/A36 return through achieved differentiation and renewed articulation. Goethe’s complete lyric supplies its own bodily and temporal movement to this relation: the changed perceiver receives a formed continuation. The shared archetypal structuration does not assign the lyric a place in an ancient myth’s geography or a stage in a chronological history.

<a id="goethe-two-ones-return"></a>

### One in change

The ratified [mytheme census] gives this poem a rich whole-page home and a light manuscript burden. Its appointed relation is One in change, returning to the native Two Ones. **Human-amplified: yes** applies to that authored appointment. The whole German sequence supplies the body through which it is developed here; an isolated translated fragment cannot perform its work alone.

The [Two Ones](../../../../../section-rooms/arguments/A11-The-Two-Ones-0-One-1-All.md) distinguish `0 = One = Self-Identity` and `1 = All = Self-Difference`. All includes each changing determination and the manifest field in which it appears. One has the source-office through which those determinations belong within a relation. Their distinct offices remain reciprocal: manifestation depends on its source, and source becomes articulated and knowable through manifestation. The poem returns a lived pressure to this native relation. Change reaches the perceiver, the body and the named identity; the concluding unity must receive those differences if it is to receive the poem at all.

The wave gives that return a local occurrence. It arrives, takes a distinguishable form and passes toward its element. In the author's appointed reading, the particular can remain real while belonging to a whole it neither originates nor possesses. The relation to [Mono/Poly](../../../../../section-rooms/arguments/A12-Mono-Poly-One-All-Whole-Many.md) preserves the changed bearer of the name, the remembered acts and the element together. Turning the element into an unchanged personal substance would discard the bodily changes through which the poem reaches it. Equating poetic water with QL's `0` would add a symbol-key that the appointment does not supply.

The poem's final gathering deepens the same relation through form. Beginning and end are joined after the body has been followed through its passing. The distinction between content in the breast and form in the mind gives the received life and its articulation different offices within the achieved whole. **Human-amplified: yes** applies to this deepening of the appointed One-in-change return, as also declared by the source house's A12/A36 relations. It does not equate the German pair word for word with the two native Ones. The content/form distinction and the source/manifest distinction remain separately stated operations.

The [integral return](../../../../../section-rooms/arguments/A36-Advent-of-Integral-Zero.md) receives a form that can carry change without pretending to restore what has passed. Reading the ending returns the reader to the first desire for an hour of arrested beauty. The intervening poem has made the desire more exact: it has included the changing person who desires, the bodily acts at stake, and the means by which an experience receives form. The opening blossom remains lost within the relation the lyric can now carry.

### Native field and the boundary of the comparison

The native operation is established in the [core theorem source](../../../../episteme/sources/internal-corpus/taylor/taylor-2026-core-theorems-pithy/taylor-2026-core-theorems-pithy.md), with its whole eight-turn field: parent `/ = −/−`, the six determinations `0/1`, `?/!`, `−/+`, `X/x`, `AM/IS`, `∞/dx`, and the returning `1/0`. Their sequence and inverse readings retain conscious circumstance, articulation, determination, personed context and local exactness within an unbounded horizon. `X/x` belongs to Taylor's language. Goethe's poem enters after that derivation as a poetic refraction, with its own temporal and bodily movement.

The [eight-determination Matheme](../../../../matheme/ql/eight-determinations.md) preserves that exact native address system. The five stanzas here are five stanzas; the six page positions carry their sequence and its authored return. No additional stanza has been manufactured to supply a numerical correspondence. The [Homology / Analogy field](../../../../episteme/etymologies/homology-and-analogy/WHOLE-FIELD.md) receives this as an operational, register-3 comparison. The return runs through the complete lyric and the native derivation, keeping their different warrants visible.

<a id="goethe-witness-and-reception"></a>

### The poem's world and its later witnesses

The German-literature home names the work's cultural and linguistic world. The valley, river, buildings and cliff belong to its narrated field; no particular geographical location is established for them here. The passing seasons and the aging body constitute the poem's time. They remain distinct from the dates through which its editions and translations have reached this project.

The Klett sheet is a Stuttgart publication of 2010, citing the Frankfurt critical edition of 1988. Those dates identify witnesses and later educational reception. The source house separately identifies Nims's 1970 magazine publication, the selected Princeton collection of 1983 and the 1994 reprint. The selected translation's exact wording remains uncollated. Its final-stanza fragment prompted the project's admission, but the fragment is neither a verified quotation from page 169 nor a recovered independent Taylor utterance. No full modern English translation is reproduced here.

The German closing words are verified at the extracted-text level of the named Klett witness; its page image and the cited critical-edition pages remain uncollated. These precise limits qualify quotation provenance. The complete German read supports the whole poetic sequence, and the native One-in-change appointment remains Argued. Other Goethe works retain their own identities: neither *Selige Sehnsucht*, *Eins und Alles* nor *Faust* substitutes for this lyric.

The whole **returns-to** [A11](../../../../../section-rooms/arguments/A11-The-Two-Ones-0-One-1-All.md) through the changed observer, the passing named wave and the gathering of beginning and end. Its declared A12 and A36 routes retain the particular life within the whole and the formed continuation of what has changed. The poem's rich field remains here, available to a light manuscript use that can return to all forty lines.
